https://www.bucksfreepress.co.uk/news/26.text: Nostalgia Marlow Marlow Bridge: The bridge which helped shape town By Heather Adams Share 0 Comments 3 Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share 0 Comments This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. Recently, Marlow Society organised its inaugural Commemorative Plaques of Marlow walk, celebrating some of the people, places and events that have helped shape the town. Over the coming months, we will be looking at some of the plaques featured on the walk. This week, we turn our attention to one of Marlow’s most familiar landmarks – Marlow Bridge, inspired by the bridge roadworks that seem to be never ending at the moment. Marlow Bridge is home to two plaques. The first celebrates the bridge itself and its fascinating connection with Hungary. The second commemorates a man who played a crucial role in ensuring that the bridge we know today was not swept away by the demands of modern traffic: Professor John Griffith. A bridge at the heart of Marlow The importance of Marlow can, in many ways, be traced back to its bridge. Marlow Bridge brought merchants to the town’s market and provided, for centuries, one of the few crossings of the river for wheeled traffic between the northern and southern banks. The original bridge stood on what is now St Peter’s Street, formerly Duck Lane. The name Duck Lane may itself have had an intriguing connection with an infamous object on the nearby wharf – the ducking stool. This was used to punish troublesome women by immersing them in the Thames, in the hope that a good soaking might cool their tempers! The early wooden bridge required constant repair and renewal. By 1828, its condition had become so poor that a survey described it as being in such a “worn out state and tottering condition” that repairing it would effectively mean replacing it. The work would require the bridge to be closed for six months. For a town dependent upon a bridge this was a serious problem. The surveyors concluded that the best long-term solution would be to build a completely new bridge. An Act of Parliament was subsequently obtained, and plans were made for a new crossing, this time further west, in line with Marlow High Street. The bridge we know today William Tierney Clark, an engineer whose reputation was rapidly growing, was the main engineer. Clark had been born in Bristol in 1783. He had already designed the Hammersmith Suspension Bridge, which opened in 1827, and Marlow Bridge was constructed on a similar principle. The road leading to the new bridge was completed in 1831 and, in the following year, the bridge was opened to traffic. The total cost came to more than £22,000 – a substantial sum at the time. Clark’s reputation went on to become international. Between 1839 and 1849, he designed the magnificent suspension bridge over the Danube connecting Buda and Pest. Known today as the Széchenyi Chain Bridge, it was Clark’s masterpiece. Marlow is twinned (or ‘bridged’) with Budapest in celebration of this link. Marlow Bridge itself regularly requires repairs over the years. But it was more than a century later that the bridge faced its greatest threat. “Marlow Bridge may have to go” By the late 1950s, the bridge was 125 years old and concerns were once again being raised about its condition. In 1957, the County Surveyor asked the Highways Committee to approach the Ministry of Transport about reducing the weight limit from five tons to just two. There were stories that the bridge might have been damaged by tanks crossing it during the Second World War, although ordinary wear and tear may have been responsible for its deteriorating condition. Whatever the cause, there was no doubt that something had to be done. The solution proposed by some was not simply to repair the bridge, but to replace it with a much larger structure capable of carrying modern traffic. By 1959, proposals included knocking out the existing arches and replacing them with much wider openings. There was even consideration of widening the bridge to accommodate heavy traffic and several lanes. To many people in Marlow, this was an alarming prospect. Among those who became determined to save the existing bridge was Professor John Griffith, a distinguished law professor at the London School of Economics who lived in Springfield Lane. Griffith later recalled that he quickly discovered that some senior officials and councillors were enthusiastic about the idea of a large new bridge. There were also modernisers in the town who supported the proposals. He feared that a new, widened bridge would do far more than simply solve a traffic problem. It would fundamentally change Marlow. A campaign to save the bridge Griffith and his supporters put forward a straightforward argument. The existing bridge was not merely an old piece of infrastructure: it was an important historic building, an intrinsic part of Marlow’s character and a key element of the town’s landscape. But there was another, equally important argument. A new bridge designed to carry heavy traffic would inevitably bring more vehicles into the centre of Marlow. Rather than solving the town’s traffic problems, it could turn the historic centre into a major thoroughfare. The campaign attracted support from many prominent local figures and organisations, including Commander Owen Wethered, Sir Evelyn Wrench, the Vicar of Marlow, solicitor Freddie Wedlake of Cripps and Shone, and Marlow Chamber of Commerce. The campaigners proposed an alternative: strengthen the existing bridge and build a bypass. They supported an increased weight limit, provided the bridge could be suitably strengthened, but opposed the proposals that would effectively destroy its historic character. In October 1960, the local press carried the alarming headline: “Marlow Bridge may have to go.” The campaign that followed was about more than bricks, mortar and engineering. It was about what kind of town Marlow wanted to become. John Griffith was the intellectual force behind the campaign. His legal mind helped articulate the case for conservation at a time when the wholesale redevelopment of historic buildings was often regarded as progress. A new bridge – but not at the expense of the old one Eventually, the compromise that campaigners had fought for was achieved. Marlow Bridge was repaired and strengthened, and in 1966 it reopened to traffic. The town retained its historic bridge rather than seeing it replaced by a modern structure. Six years later, in 1972, the Marlow bypass and its own new bridge opened, providing the alternative route for through traffic that Griffith and his fellow campaigners had advocated. The result is something that can easily be taken for granted today. Heavy traffic can bypass the town, while pedestrians, cyclists and vehicles can continue to cross the Thames on the beautiful suspension bridge that has been part of Marlow’s identity for nearly two centuries. Remembering John Griffith John Griffith was not simply a campaigner for an attractive old bridge. He was a significant academic and legal thinker whose work challenged conventional ideas about the judiciary and the establishment. He loved Marlow and its historic buildings and recognised something that can be easy to overlook: once a historic landmark has gone, it cannot simply be recreated. Griffith was a founding member of the Marlow Society, established in the aftermath of the campaign to save the bridge in 1960. Its purpose was to “protect, develop, improve and promote features of history or public interest” in Marlow and the surrounding parishes – a mission that continues today. Today, thousands of people cross Marlow Bridge without knowing how close it once came to disappearing. The elegant structure has become such an inseparable part of the town that it is difficult to imagine Marlow without it. The plaque commemorating Professor John Griffith is not simply a tribute to one man. It is a reminder that the character of a town is shaped not only by the buildings and landscapes that have survived from the past, but also by the people who care enough to fight for them. Information on future Walks and Talks organised by the Marlow Society, can be found on the website. Photograph: Sener Yilmaz Aslan/Getty Images Opinion France The Guardian view on the French school protests: the political class needs to heed the voice of students Editorial A generation facing unprecedented challenges deserves better than an underfunded education system Tue 6 Oct 2026 14.31 EDT Last modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 18.06 EDT Share O ne of the most famous slogans in France’s May 1968 student protests declared “ L’imagination au pouvoir ” (Power to the imagination). In a postwar context of steady growth, the ’68ers dreamed of shaping an egalitarian society, freed from the social constraints of their parents’ generation. Nearly five decades on, in a very different economic climate, the goal for most of the tens of thousands of pupils disrupting schools across the country is more modest. As one placard on display had it: “I’d like to be worrying about my maths exam, not my future”. A huge turnout of hundreds of thousands of protesters on Tuesday – a number that included many parents and teachers – confirmed the depth of resentment at years of budget cuts leading to crumbling school buildings, overcrowded classes and chronic staff shortages. Other complaints point to a lack of resources to deal with the now frequent heatwaves that make classrooms intolerable in May and June, and the unfairness of an opaque, algorithmically driven selection process for universities. Confronted by the anxieties of a generation facing challenges ranging from the climate emergency to the impact of AI on future job opportunities, the response of Emmanuel Macron’s government has been disastrously heavy-handed. Instead of being instructed to show maximum restraint, given the age of most of those involved, security forces were urged to intervene to break up the school “blockades”. The result has been heightened confrontation and unacceptable violence on both sides. More than 200 students have been injured, as well as over 700 police officers and a number of teachers. One 15-year-old boy had his hand blown off during a protest in Lens, another lost an eye, and more than 4,000 minors were taken into custody, with nearly 1,500 facing prosecution. At a political level, the eruption of anger over the underfunding of education has underlined the folly of Mr Macron’s ongoing attempt to balance France’s books by taking an axe to social spending. During his chaotic second term as president, five prime ministers have attempted to force through austerity budgets in order to cut the deficit and satisfy increasingly restive bond markets. The latest, Sébastien Lecornu, has belatedly said that the students’ core demands should be addressed. But last month he proposed cuts worth €54bn, including a real-terms reduction in schools funding. A credible approach would require more resources, not less. Six months out from a presidential election in which Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner, the spectacle of burned-out schools, baton rounds and teargassed protesters feels ominous. As French politics polarises amid a crisis of faith in mainstream leaders, Ms Le Pen has accused the hard left of fomenting the school protests and called for a toughening up of “anti-riot” legislation. Public sector workers were on the streets on Tuesday, demonstrating against wage freezes. The major unions are jointly planning further demonstrations for November. An autumn of discontent now seems possible, as a lame-duck government enters its final months. Mass protest in the streets is hardly an unknown phenomenon in France. But as calls mount for government spending to be further cut to appease market sentiment, the scale and intensity of the school protests should be heeded by the political class. As the social contract in France comes under increasing strain, the voice of its protesting students needs to be heard.
